name: Mikhail Gorbachev
role: Soviet leader (1985–1991), USSR president (1990–1991) and later social-democratic advocate
summary: Gorbachev’s mature outlook combined competitive democracy, civil freedoms and a socially regulated market economy. He promoted disarmament, international cooperation and environmental protection, while his later support for Crimea’s transfer to Russia reflected his emphasis on the referendum’s claimed popular choice.

arms-reduction.rationale: He demanded reversing the arms race and reducing nuclear and other weapons arsenals.

central-planning.rationale: He said returning to a planned economy would not help Russia.

consent-of-governed.rationale: He demanded honest elections and periodic turnover of those in power.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: He urged overcoming hyper-consumption and reshaping social values.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: He criticised cutting social programmes instead of investing in human well-being.

democracy-best.rationale: In 2016 he insisted there was no alternative to democracy.

direct-action.rationale: He supported environmental protest drawing attention to problems while personally rejecting some Greenpeace methods.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: In 2014 he explicitly defended peoples’ right to decide territorial destiny by referendum.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: He demanded strict state standards and large-scale investment to address climate change urgently.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: He called for stronger UN cooperation, international law and collective responses to global challenges.

equal-outcomes.rationale: He condemned wage-levelling and warned against equating social justice with crude egalitarianism, while defending a floor of social guarantees.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: He treated the danger of nuclear war as the most urgent problem requiring immediate joint action.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: He criticised subsidies for fossil-fuel industries instead of the energy sector of the future.

expand-nuclear.rationale: He rejected immediate abandonment but called for a rapid shift toward safer renewable alternatives.

free-basic-services-for-all.rationale: He listed free education and free medical services among socialism's guarantees for everyone and defended them as gains.

future-generations.rationale: He explicitly accepted responsibility for preserving a future for grandchildren and great-grandchildren.

gradual-change.rationale: In 1988 he warned against restructuring everything at one fell swoop and spoke of working step by step, yet he repeatedly called perestroika a radical, revolutionary transformation.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: He allowed national forms of democracy while insisting on universal democratic essentials.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: He defended universal freedom of political choice and rejected imposed political systems.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: He sought negotiated nuclear reductions toward a nuclear-free world rather than indefinite retention.

leader-cult.rationale: He welcomed Khrushchev’s exposure of Stalin’s cult as a step toward human freedom.

limit-growth.rationale: He demanded replacing environmentally destructive economic expansion with production of sustainable social goods.

local-essentials-public.rationale: He opposed deregulating water resources while allowing regulated participation by public and private providers.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: He accepted markets while rejecting an economy governed solely by profit without public control.

military-superiority.rationale: He reaffirmed the pledge that neither Russia nor the United States should seek military superiority.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: He urged at least privileged status for Chechnya within the Russian Federation.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: He accepted national, local and international companies contributing to water provision under public safeguards.

nation-first.rationale: He placed common human interests above exclusive national or class priorities in international politics.

night-watchman-state.rationale: He rejected excluding the state from economic life and defended socially oriented market governance.

one-party-rule.rationale: He defined competition between political parties as indispensable to democracy.

party-controls-media.rationale: He defended a free, responsible press and criticised damage to independent television.

pay-for-effort.rationale: He demanded pay according to the work done and its end results and the uprooting of wage-levelling, which comes close to pay by effort without naming it.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: He criticised Russian media’s continued dependence on corporate ownership.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: At the UN in 1988 he said democratic patterns should not be pressed on others and that democracy when exported often loses its values, placing freedom of choice first.

public-ownership.rationale: In 1989 he pictured a society built on a variety of forms of public ownership, but in 1991 he listed the total domination of centrally managed state property among the causes of stagnation.

regulate-corporations.rationale: He demanded social and state control over an economy detached from social concerns.

return-lost-territory.rationale: He endorsed Crimea’s return to Russia as the peninsula’s chosen outcome.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: He demanded rich countries provide major financial and technical climate assistance to developing countries.

right-to-secede.rationale: His 2014 comments defended territorial choice by referendum, without articulating an unconditional right in every case.

separate-church-state.rationale: He cited Lenin's decree separating church from state and school from church as the basis of relations with believers, and ruled out administrative pressure on them.

separated-powers.rationale: He demanded a constitutional balance between the three government branches.

state-directs-investment.rationale: He called for public mobilisation of resources toward low-carbon technology and renewable energy.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: He said the non-materialist outlook of believers deserves respect and that disagreeing with it is no reason for administrative pressure to assert materialist views.

strong-leader.rationale: He urged Russia to overcome excessive dependence on its leaders.

suppress-opposition.rationale: He defended political competition, civil society and basic freedoms.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: He described modern technological risk and required public oversight rather than relying on technology alone.

term-limits.rationale: He criticised rulers staying too long and warned against Putin seeking another presidency.

troops-home-from-abroad.rationale: In 1988 he announced unilateral cuts that withdrew Soviet troops and tanks from allied countries in Europe, and in 1991 he cited foreign troops leaving other countries as progress.

universal-healthcare.rationale: He named free medical services among the social guarantees that socialism provides and treated them as gains to keep while the economy was reformed.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: He opposed entrenched leadership and urged limits to presidential incumbency in practice.

war-builds-character.rationale: He argued modern wars cannot resolve humanity’s central problems and must be outlawed.

worker-farmer-alliance.rationale: He called the alliance between the working class and the peasantry a fundamental question of the Party's policy and of the cooperative movement.

notes: Later democratic and social-democratic commitments override earlier Soviet orthodoxy. Crimea answers record his stated assessment, not a finding that the disputed 2014 vote was free or lawful. Calls for disarmament are distinguished from immediate unilateral abolition. Modern social and digital-policy questions remain null where his record is not sufficiently specific. Pass of 2026-11-19 (claude-sonnet-5-5): read Gorbachev’s 1988–90 speeches and reports on marxists.org (19th Party Conference, July 1988 plenum, agrarian policy, party work, UN address) and his Nobel lecture; searched economy, government, world, liberty and ecology themes. The new statements are null except those cited.
